In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
no one country has a perfect solution for the problem of cancer care.

the USA has not yet developed a formalized process for the assessment of new drugs, but it has been a pioneer in the development of new cancer agents and has been the first country to approve many of these drugs.

the USA is not alone in its struggles with access to cancer drugs, and that the UK, Canada, and Australia, all with socialized health systems and active health-technology assessment programmes, have similar challenges.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is no “one size fits all” model for the optimal cancer drug policy.
the USA is not alone in facing the challenge of balancing the need to improve patient care with the need for sustainability in health care spending.

the USA is not immune to the rising cost of cancer care and that there is a need for the USA to adopt a more systematic and transparent process for the assessment of new drugs, similar to that in other countries.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the USA should take note of the experiences and lessons learned from these other countries, as they are likely to be relevant to the current debate on how to best ensure value for money and patient access in a changing cancer care environment.
, despite the different mechanisms for access to cancer drugs, all countries have a shared concern for the sustainability of their respective systems.
